The tides are, at their heart, a story about gravity pulling unevenly. The Moon tugs on the Earth, but it doesn't tug equally everywhere. The side of our planet facing the Moon feels a stronger gravitational pull than the center, and the center feels a stronger pull than the far side. This difference in force stretches the Earth and, more visibly, stretches the oceans. Water on the near side gets pulled toward the Moon, forming a bulge. Water on the far side, meanwhile, is left behind as the solid Earth is tugged slightly more strongly than it is, creating a second bulge pointing away from the Moon. So at any given moment, two great swells of water sit on opposite sides of the globe.

As the Earth spins beneath these bulges roughly once a day, a coastline passes through one bulge, then the trough between them, then the other bulge, then the next trough. That rotation is what gives most places two high tides and two low tides each day, spaced about twelve hours and twenty-five minutes apart. The extra twenty-five minutes exist because the Moon is also moving in its orbit, so the Earth has to turn a little further to bring the same coastline back under the same bulge.
